doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Orchestral saxophone parts and Pictures at an Exhibition
summary: Rowe and Ricker discuss rest-heavy sax solos, Rachmaninoff's Symphonic Dances and a nerve-racking soprano sax part in a mixed Pictures at an Exhibition.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, to sit in the middle of all that. I wonder if you’ve ever had the experience of playing specifically a saxophone in an orchestra? The reason I’m asking is this happened to me once. I believe the piece was by a fellow named Honneger. And there was an alto sax part and of course the part required you to sit there for probably 80 bars and then come in and of course it’s a solo. And it wasn’t the kind of music that you could just feel
where you are. Like is this measure 49 or is it 50 of my rests. Is this something that ever happened to you?

Oh yeah. Yeah that’s happened. But that’s part of the deal. That happens in Rachmaninoff’s Symphonic Dances you know the only thing the alto saxophone does is play a solo. It’s in a bunch of sharps and you play it at about, I don’t know, about ten minutes into the piece. So you’re there, your reed is dried out, could have lost suction, you know you never know what’s going to happen there. But I’ll tell you one of the roughest things the “Pictures at an Exhibition” was written by Mussorgsky, okay? And it was the most famous version, the orchestration of it, is by Ravel. That’s the one that everybody knows. And that’s the one that has the big saxophone solo in it that’s “The Old Castle.” So the thing is this Mussorgsky piece has been arranged probably, well I think I heard the number 25 times. So one of the conductors, or our main conductor, had the idea we’re going to do “Pictures at an Exhibition,” but we’re going to mix and match the various variations. And he took about four or five or maybe six composers and put them in. Okay so the saxophone, normally you play alto saxophone, nice melodic thing, it’s a great solo. The part I had to play on soprano saxophone was a trumpet part and it goes like this [scats] that kind of thing like that, keep them going so on soprano sax I think it starts on a high C or something. And so I’m telling you, that was a killer. An absolute killer. And I was really nervous about that. But I blew it the first time around, I played it so fast. Because the trumpet players usually play it real fast. And I talked to the conductor and I said, “I’m sorry I got way ahead.” And I said, “I thought we’d be going faster.” And he said, “Oh the trumpets just like to play it fast to get through it.” He said, “We’re going to go slower.” So anyway, that’s a lot of pressure on you and that’s the way it is.
That whole mindset of playing exactly what someone else has written and being in the jazz world is, I don’t have an exact comment except it’s such as different way of being in your head.

Yeah it is, but yeah, there’s different rules. There’s different rules. You know if you crack a note in a jazz thing it’s not that big a deal you know. But you crack a note in the middle of a legit solo it’s pretty big.
